articles.title: Idaho Killer’s Unsealed Psych Report Reveals Four New Diagnoses
articles.description: Idaho Department of Corrections / via REUTERS A detailed psych evaluation of accused multiple Idaho killer Bryan Kohberger has been released by a court revealing eight mental health-related disorders that Kohberger has reportedly struggled with. The information was released Thursday just weeks after Kohberger declared that he intends to withdraw his guilty plea in the horrific 2022 killings of four University of Idaho students. An expert hired by Kohberger’s defense team, Rachel Lawson Orr, conducted the evaluation. Four of Kohberger’s diagnoses—Autism, OCD, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder and the eating disorder Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder—are detailed in the newly released report from February 2025, People reported. Orr concluded that Kohberger also met the criteria of an additional four diagnoses in the past that were previously undisclosed: Developmental Coordination Disorder, an unspecified depressive disorder, anorexia nervosa, and Opioid Use Disorder. Kohberger insisted in a statement last month on his “actual innocence,” and claimed the prosecution’s case against him was a “myopic narrative work of fiction.” Kohberger had agreed last year to serve four consecutive life sentences without parole to avoid capital punishment. Kristi Goncalves, 48, the mother of murder victim Kaylee Goncalves, attacked Kohberger for “playing games” with his plan to retract his guilty plea. “America has seen our family go through pain for many, many years now,” she told Newsweek . Read it at PEOPLE Read more at The Daily Beast.

articles.title: Date workers toil through rising heat in Sindh
articles.description: KHAIRPUR: In blazing temperatures, Muhammad Idrees ladles boiled dates from a vat simmering over an open flame, work that labourers lament is getting hotter each year in Sindh. Date season arrives in July, when temperatures in the province regularly hit the mid-40 degrees Celsius. Workers start before sunrise, and split the day into short shifts, but the heat soon catches up with them. Their gruelling routine involves harvesting and boiling fruit picked from palms that line Khairpur district, which produces more than half the country’s dates and supports thousands of farmers and seasonal labourers. Labourers begin work around 2am to avoid the worst of the daytime heat Idrees, who has worked the date harvest for more than a decade, said the heat has now become “unbearable”. Date labourers are one of many professions in Pakistan that are becoming more difficult and dangerous as temperatures rise. “It used to be less intense,” Idrees told AFP as temperatures hit 42°C. “The heat is much harsher and the days are extremely hot. We fall ill because of it.” Multiple workers said they often suffer heatstroke, fainting and fever. “When the heat makes us sick, we go to the doctor for treatment and then return to work,” Idrees added. Pakistan is among the countries globally most vulnerable to climate change despite contributing less than one per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions. The country has experienced increasingly frequent heatwaves, erratic monsoon rains and devastating floods, including catastrophic 2022 floods that inundated around one-third of the country and displaced millions, hitting Sindh particularly hard. Heat and harvest Workers descend on date farms to begin work around 2am to avoid the worst of the daytime heat and take a break before continuing until the late evening. Idrees said the physically demanding work earns him around Rs1,200, roughly $4, a day. “We harvest the dates, load them onto trolleys and bring them here,” he said. “They are boiled over the fire and then spread outside in the sun to dry.” Pakistan, the world’s fifth-largest date producer, normally earns more than $120 million a year in exports, according to industry estimates. Date farmer Shahnawaz Phulpoto, who owns more than 1,500 palm trees, said that heavy monsoon rains from shifting weather patterns have hampered date crops and caused financial losses. But for now the main challenge is the heat, he added, as the sun blazed overhead. “The temperature rises every year,” he said, adding: “We are seeing the effects of climate change every year.” Published in Dawn, August 15th, 2026

articles.title: LETTER: Digging deeper on U.S. firearm deaths
LETTER: Questions about the death of a Metro officer
Death in Karachi
articles.description: ON the night of Aug 13, 2026, Mir Raza Ali’s father was on TV imploring — as he had been doing for some time — for justice. It is now over two weeks since Mir Raza Ali, a 25-year-old businessman, left his home on an ill-fated trip that would be his last. The gruesome nature of his death, questions surrounding the initial police investigation and the inconsistent behaviour of the officials demonstrate why parents in Karachi so fear their children leaving their homes. In this sense, there are at least three dimensions to the death of Mir Raza Ali. First is the immense grief and the individual tragedy faced by the family of the young man. The death of one so young is heartbreaking enough, but the horrific details of this case and the mystery that surrounds those who appeared to have tortured and killed him have deepened the tragedy. Second is the story of lapses in the investigation of his death and the dismissive attitude of Karachi’s police force towards the violent deaths of young people. Third, there is the message that the ongoing disclosures and delays convey to the people of an exhausted and neglected city. The violent death of Mir Raza Ali has gripped the city. Here was a young man who did not leave the country despite having the opportunity to do so. Mir Raza was a business wunderkind, starting a business on next to nothing as an 18-year-old and making it a resounding success. In interviews, Mir Raza leveraged this fact as evidence that there is hope for the young in Karachi and the rest of the country. He created jobs for scores of people. One of them, holding a placard at Karachi’s Teen Talwar area, could not stop his tears when talking about just how well-mannered, professional and respectful the young man had been. If the family had not been able to somehow set up a protest movement — and Karachi’s police surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed had not been so blunt in noting deficiencies in the initial postmortem — Mir Raza Ali’s death might have continued to be treated as possible suicide. The second postmortem found multiple injuries, including fractures and a wound caused by a bullet entering from the back; a murder charge was subsequently added. We now come to the second dimension of the case: the lapses and negligence that have so far come to light. As such failures are uncovered, they underscore the impunity with which the institutional structure can frustrate efforts at investigating homicide in the city. A judicial commission was proposed but deferred after the family expressed confidence in a new police investigation team. The level of protection available to officials who fail in their duties seems to be so formidable that few appear bothered enough to even provide convincing justifications for their actions. This situation reflects a collapse of the administrative system and a hollowing out of democratic institutions to say the least. No one is more alone than a victim of crime in Karachi. The third and most pernicious aspect is the message that this case and others like it send to those living in the city. Karachi denizens are used to living life in defensive mode. On the surface, things seem to function. Drive around the city at night and restaurants are full, people are shopping, traffic is everywhere — but life is merely a thread away from being extinguished. No one is more alone than a citizen of Karachi who has become a victim of crime. If your home is robbed, your child is missing or your money is stolen, you are immediately alone. The idea of justice has become anathema. Even if you want an FIR registered for a robbery, you may have to bribe the police; it follows that when som­eone is killed, few believe justice will be brought to the perpetrators. This latest case just substantiates the feeling of futility and resignation that casts its shadow over millions of people. Changing medical boards, changing hypotheses of the case, changing investigation officials, selectively releasing information, officials saying one thing and then nothing — all show how unsafe and broken this city has become. Investigative teams, medical boards, postmortem reports, DNA and toxicology findings imply that the data gathered will hopefully lead to some conclusion, and perhaps closure. But the point is that, all too often, there is no point at all. The powerful and indifferent wait it out until the blood dries on the ground and there are new murders to ignore or pass off as suicides. Perhaps the definition of being suicidal in Karachi is simply staying in the city. The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy. rafia.zakaria@gmail.com Published in Dawn, August 15th, 2026
